result: The ordinary least squares method, introduced by Legendre and Gauss over 200 years ago, is ubiquitous in analyzing two-dimensional scatter plots but requires assuming one variable depends on another. However, in many cases, particularly in biological systems, relationships between variables are more complex and such assumptions may not be valid.

result: When data points do not fall on a straight line, the three regression methods (vertical residuals, horizontal residuals, and perpendicular residuals) produce different best-fitting lines with shallow, steep, and intermediate slopes, respectively, and these lines will not coincide except when R² = 1.

result: The relationship between R² and the slopes of the two ordinary least squares regression lines is mathematically defined: R² equals the ratio of the two slopes, and as R² decreases from 1 to 0, the slopes diverge from equality to 0 and infinity.
status_reasoning: Claim C11 contains a mathematical error. R² is NOT equal to the slope of y-on-x divided by the slope of x-on-y. Rather, R² equals the product of these two slopes (or equivalently, the square of either slope times the other). This fundamental error undermines claims C12-C14, which depend on this incorrect relationship, even though the qualitative behavior described (divergence with decreasing R²) is correct.

result: Analysis of Ressler et al. data shows that individual regression lines (y on x or x on y) do not fully capture data trends, but plotting all three lines provides a fuller picture, with the orthogonal regression appearing to more accurately describe the trend.
